newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces scepticism in war on corruption.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces scepticism in war on corruption.

text.p: It starts with a bottle of vodka or a wad of roubles stuffed into a lowly official's hand, but corruption goes right to the top in Russia and few people believe President Boris Yeltsin can wipe it out now.
By declaring war on graft on Thursday, Yeltsin took on the scourge of Russia since tsarist times and something that is as much a way of life here as vodka, cabbage and fur hats.

"If you don't smooth your path, you won't get anywhere," says to a Russian proverb aptly describing the importance of bribes. The Russian language has dozens of words to describe bribery, corruption and greasing of palms.
As long as 300 years ago, Peter the Great set sail for the Netherlands telling his entourage to sew up their pockets to avoid the temptation to steal or take bribes.

Corruption survived communist times and bribes can still be required to secure anything from preferential medical treatment to getting items through customs. Ordinary people openly discuss how university places can be bought and swap stories on the size of the latest "fines" they have had to pay traffic police.
Moscow's liberal ex-mayor Gavriil Popov, tired of fighting corruption, offered once to legalise it by letting officials set "charges" for their services. The idea was never taken up.
Yeltsin knows how difficult a task he faces but has identified corruption as one of the people's main concerns and believes he will boost his flagging popularity if he succeeds.

He vowed in a radio address to ensure openness in how state funds are spent, abolish tax and customs benefits, open up the system of tendering for state orders and overhaul the state administration. A new code is planned for civil servants.
"I appeal to leaders at every level. Today as never before, it is necessary to carefully select personnel, to expel officials who have not lived up to expectations," he said.
By attacking corruption, Yeltsin wants to show he is ready to get tough to put Russia's house in order after months on the political sidelines with ill health.

Economic reforms are unlikely to progress fast if corruption continues at all levels of officialdom and his reform-minded new government, unveiled in the past few weeks, fails to cut decisively through Russia's notorious red tape.
But few politicians or ordinary Russians believe Yeltsin can make much headway with what is only the latest of several wars he has declared on corruption.

"We have seen 'clean hands' operations in the past. Usually they don't get the big corrupters but some small officials. I think this campaign will probably be the same," human rights campaigner Valery Abramkin told a news conference.
Alexei Ilyushenko, then acting prosecutor-general, was charged last year with bribery. Several generals were sacked this week and accused of bribery. All deny the charges.
Most people believe many more senior officials are corrupt but are protected in high places. Few top officials are officially charged or jailed.

"This is far from the first attempt to fight corruption," centrist parliamentarian Sergei Belyayev, a government supporter, told Interfax news agency. "It is not enough just to make declarations on such things."

Agrarian leader Nikolai Kharitonov agreed. He said Boris Nemtsov, the first deputy prime minister closely associated with the anti-crime drive, "might turn out to be a Don Quixote who fights windmills", evoking the naive literary hero.
Parliamentarians found little new in Yeltsin's latest plans and noted that Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov has said that emergency measures will not be used to crack down on corruption.
"We have above all to change a lot in our own heads first, so the fight against corruption will be long and hard," liberal parliamentarian Vladimir Lukin told Itar-Tass news agency.
